> Continuing the structured testing pass. As before, this comment is from Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode.

Retested on `@flue/sdk@0.3.4` + `@flue/cli@0.3.4` (and confirmed identical behavior on 0.3.3). The fixes don't work — the same `TypeError: The RPC receiver does not implement the method "createSessionEnv"` reproduces end-to-end on a fresh deploy.

## Why neither `instanceof` check matches

I added a probe agent that runs inside the deployed worker and inspects the value `getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id)` returns. Results:

```json
{
  "isInstanceSandbox": false,           // 0.3.3's check
  "isInstanceDurableObject": false,     // 0.3.4's check
  "protoName": "DurableObject",
  "protoProtoName": "Fetcher",
  "typeofSb": "object",
  "typeofExec": "function",
  "typeofCreateSessionEnv": "function", // proxy lies
  "hasExec": true,
  "hasCreateSessionEnv": true,          // proxy lies
  "SandboxName": "Sandbox",
  "DurableObjectName": "DurableObject"
}
```

The proxy's prototype `constructor.name` is the *string* `"DurableObject"`, but the constructor object is a workerd-internal class with a different identity than the one user code imports from `cloudflare:workers`. They are name-equivalent but not identity-equivalent. `instanceof` checks identity, so it returns false.

Same pattern as 0.3.3's `instanceof Sandbox` failure: the user-importable class and the runtime stub class share a name but not an identity.

**Conclusion: no `instanceof` check against any user-importable class can reliably identify a `getSandbox()` RPC stub.**

## Reproduction (clean)

```ts
// agents/container.ts
import type { FlueContext } from '@flue/sdk/client';
import { getSandbox } from '@cloudflare/sandbox';

export const triggers = { webhook: true };

export default async function ({ init, id, env }: FlueContext) {
  const sandbox = getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id);
  const agent = await init({ sandbox, model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6' });
  const session = await agent.session();
  return { uname: (await session.shell('uname -a')).stdout };
}
```

`wrangler.jsonc` with the standard `Sandbox`-named DO + container binding from the deploy guide. Deploy and POST → 500 with the `createSessionEnv` TypeError.

## Suggested fixes that should actually work

A few options that don't rely on runtime identity checks against the proxy:

**1. Build-time wiring (cleanest).** The Flue build already detects `Sandbox`-named DO bindings — that's where the `[flue] Detected Sandbox-named DO binding "Sandbox"` log line comes from. Have the generated `_entry.ts` directly call `cfSandboxToSessionEnv` whenever the user passes the result of `getSandbox()` *for that specific binding*. This requires wrapping the user's `init({ sandbox })` call so the SDK can know the value came from a Cloudflare sandbox binding. Concretely: don't try to detect at runtime — generate a wrapper that *knows* a given DO binding is a CF sandbox.

**2. Documented manual escape hatch.** Export `cfSandboxToSessionEnv` as the official happy path:

```ts
import { cfSandboxToSessionEnv } from '@flue/sdk/cloudflare';
const sandbox = await cfSandboxToSessionEnv(getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id));
const agent = await init({ sandbox: { createSessionEnv: async () => sandbox } });
```

…or better, make `init` accept a pre-built `SessionEnv` directly so users don't need the wrapper-of-wrapper. This documents the layering honestly: the user calls Flue's CF helper themselves, no magic detection.

**3. Heuristic detection that actually works.** The proxy's proto chain has `constructor.name === "DurableObject"` and `Object.getPrototypeOf(proto).constructor.name === "Fetcher"`. Checking `Object.getPrototypeOf(sandbox)?.constructor?.name === "DurableObject"` would match. This is fragile (relies on workerd internals naming) but works today and is at least honest about being heuristic.

I'd advocate for **(1) plus (2)** — make the documented happy path work via build-time wiring, and expose the manual hatch for users who construct things in non-standard ways.

## Other notes from this retest

- `@flue/sdk@0.3.4`'s entry template has a clear comment block explaining why structural duck-typing and `instanceof <UserSandboxClass>` don't work, then asserts `instanceof DurableObject` is "the only check that actually identifies a CF sandbox stub." The comment is correct about the first two; it's incorrect about the third. The runtime probe proves this.

- `client.mjs`'s `isSandboxFactory` still trusts the lying proxy (returns true for any `'X' in stub`), which is what causes the actual crash. After `resolveSandbox` returns null, control falls through to `isSandboxFactory`, which says "yes" to anything, and Flue tries to call `Sandbox.createSessionEnv` over RPC. So even fixing `resolveSandbox` would still leave a footgun if a non-CF user passes any object with a `createSessionEnv`-shaped property.

- I confirmed the wrapper code path *does* work when called manually: `cfSandboxToSessionEnv(getSandbox(env.Sandbox, id))` produces a working `SessionEnv` whose `exec`/`readFile`/etc. methods I was able to call successfully. So the *plumbing* in 0.3.4 is correct — only the routing into it is broken.

When I removed the manual migrations workaround from `wrangler.jsonc` and let Flue auto-generate, the output **changed shape** — instead of one `flue-v1` blob containing every class:

```jsonc
"migrations": [
  { "tag": "flue-class-AgentsmdTest", "new_sqlite_classes": ["AgentsmdTest"] },
  { "tag": "flue-class-Chat",         "new_sqlite_classes": ["Chat"] },
  { "tag": "flue-class-Container",    "new_sqlite_classes": ["Container"] },
  { "tag": "flue-class-Echo",         "new_sqlite_classes": ["Echo"] },
  // ... one per class
]
```

This is the right shape — per-class deterministic tags. **Adding a new agent will only emit a new `flue-class-<NewName>` tag, leaving the others untouched. The redeploy-churn problem in this issue's body is fixed.** Thanks!

## Two remaining gaps

### 1. User-declared `Sandbox` class isn't included in auto-generated migrations

In my run, the bindings included `Sandbox` (the `@cloudflare/sandbox` class re-exported per deploy-guide instructions), but the auto-generated migrations did **not** include any tag for it. So a fresh deploy following the deploy guide:

```jsonc
{
  "durable_objects": { "bindings": [{ "class_name": "Sandbox", "name": "Sandbox" }] },
  "containers": [{ "class_name": "Sandbox", "image": "./Dockerfile" }]
  // ... no migrations field
}
```

…would produce a `dist/wrangler.jsonc` with `flue-class-<each-agent>` tags but **no migration for the `Sandbox` class itself**. Cloudflare requires every DO class to have a migration; `wrangler deploy` would fail. The deploy guide should mention this, or Flue's auto-merge should detect Sandbox-named bindings and emit a tag for them too.

### 2. Migration scheme transition story for existing deploys

For users who deployed on the old `flue-v1` scheme (anyone before this fix landed), upgrading to a Flue version that emits the new `flue-class-X` scheme will fail at deploy because the new tags will conflict with the already-applied `flue-v1` tag on Cloudflare's side. A user migrating off the broken old scheme has to:

1. Pin a manual `migrations` block matching what Cloudflare already has.
2. Add new classes via additional manual tags (which is exactly the workaround documented in this issue's body).

That's not the end of the world, but it would help to have a one-time migration script (e.g. `flue migrate-migrations`) or doc note like "if you previously deployed on `flue-v1`-style migrations, pin them manually in your `wrangler.jsonc` to retain compatibility — Flue will leave a manual migrations block untouched on rebuild." (I confirmed it does pass through manual blocks unchanged in my testing — but a doc note saying so would unblock anyone caught in this transition.)

## Summary

- ✅ Per-class deterministic tag scheme — fixes the original redeploy issue.
- ❌ Sandbox class missing from auto-generated migrations.
- ❌ No migration story for existing-`flue-v1`-deploy users.

I'd say this issue can be closed once the Sandbox-class gap is addressed (or documented). The transition story is a smaller nice-to-have.

Verified the container path is the working escape hatch for this issue. Tested on `@flue/[email protected]` after #20 was fixed, with the corrected Dockerfile (see #21).

## A/B verification

**Negative case** (bare container image, no `COPY`):

```dockerfile
FROM docker.io/cloudflare/sandbox:0.9.2
```

Result: `/workspace/` is empty, `session.skill('greet')` errors with `Skill "greet" not registered. Available: (none).` — same failure as the default virtual sandbox in this issue's repro. AGENTS.md test (the magic-phrase test from CP10 on this project's TEST-LOG) returns the LLM's literal observation that the file isn't there.

**Positive case** (image COPYs workspace files):

```dockerfile
FROM docker.io/cloudflare/sandbox:0.9.2
COPY .agents /workspace/.agents
COPY AGENTS.md /workspace/AGENTS.md
```

Result:
- `session.skill('greet', { args: { name: 'Container' }, result: v.object({ greeting: v.string() }) })` → `{"greeting": "Welcome, Container — ..."}`. Works.
- `session.prompt('What is the magic phrase?', { result: ... })` → `{"reply": "the password is \`BANANA\`"}`. AGENTS.md is loaded into the system prompt.

So the container path with explicit `COPY` is the working escape hatch for skills + AGENTS.md today.

## Why this isn't fully resolved by the workaround

Even with the container workaround verified, this issue's body is still substantively true:

1. **The default virtual sandbox is still broken.** Skills + AGENTS.md silently don't load there. That's the primary surface a new user lands on (per `start.md`) and the guidance in this issue's body still applies.
2. **The container workaround is undocumented.** The deploy guide's example Dockerfile (a) doesn't COPY skills/AGENTS.md, and (b) is wrong on a deeper level — see #21. So even users who try containers don't get skills working unless they figure out both the right base image AND the COPY.
3. **No `init({ skills })` escape hatch.** Still a real DX gap for users who want skills without containers / R2.

## Suggested doc-side action (regardless of code fix)

Update the deploy guide's `Container agents` section's example Dockerfile to:

```dockerfile
FROM docker.io/cloudflare/sandbox:0.9.2
COPY .agents /workspace/.agents
COPY AGENTS.md /workspace/AGENTS.md
```

…with a sentence explaining that this makes skills + AGENTS.md available inside the container (and that they don't load on the default virtual sandbox). This is mostly free DX once #21's Dockerfile fix lands.

## Suggested code-side fixes (mostly carryover from this issue's original body)

1. `init({ skills, agentsMd })` API option — the cleanest fix; works on every sandbox.
2. Build-time bundling: `flue build` could COPY `.agents/` and `AGENTS.md` into a Layer the user's image inherits from, or generate a Dockerfile snippet, or warn when these files exist in the workspace but aren't COPY'd into the user's image.
3. Lazy re-discovery on `session.skill()` cache miss — would let `session.shell()` setup before `session.skill()` work.

## Status

I'd recommend keeping this issue open until either #1 above or the deploy-guide doc update lands. The container workaround is verified-working but not discoverable.

Closing this. Two fixes landed; the broader architectural changes proposed here were considered and intentionally rejected. Reasoning below.

## What landed

1. **Improved runtime error in `session.skill()`** (`packages/sdk/src/session.ts`). The error now names the conventional path (`<cwd>/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`), states the init-time loading rule, and explains why the default empty sandbox has no skills. Users who hit the failure now see exactly where the line is and why.
2. **Reframed the `## Sandbox context` section** in `docs/deploy-cloudflare.md`. Skills and `AGENTS.md` are now described as **optional** workspace-context files \u2014 not features the empty sandbox is "missing." The loading rule is stated up front, before the example. The framing is non-prescriptive: how you populate the sandbox depends on which sandbox you're using, with examples (R2 upload, container `COPY`, `session.shell()` on a sandbox you control) given as illustration rather than a closed list.

## What was considered and rejected

- **Build-time bundling of skills/`AGENTS.md`** (alongside roles). Roles are agent-static config that describe behavior the agent has across all sandboxes; skills and `AGENTS.md` are runtime workspace context tied to whatever sandbox the agent is operating against. The asymmetry is intentional, not an oversight. Unifying them would conflate two different concerns.
- **`init({ skills, agentsMd })`** programmatic injection. Workarounds already exist for the dynamic-skills case: a custom `BashFactory` can seed `InMemoryFs` before `init()`, remote sandboxes have their own setup APIs (R2 upload, container `COPY`, etc.), and most users who reach for skills will have static files baked in by some prior step anyway. Adding the API for a niche use case isn't worth the surface area.
- **`agent.reloadContext()` / `session.reloadContext()`** to support a `session.shell()`-then-skills workflow. Agent-level reload would mutate `agentConfig` that's shared by reference across sessions, including in-flight ones \u2014 a real correctness hazard. Session-level reload reintroduces per-session context divergence, which is a debugging footgun. The need is rare and workarounds exist.
- **Moving context discovery from `init()` to `agent.session()`**. Closes the shell-setup loop architecturally but taxes the common case (every session pays discovery cost), allows different sessions of the same agent to have different skill lists, and muddies the "init is heavy, sessions are cheap" mental model. Not worth it for a niche workflow.

## On the original framing

Two specific claims in the issue body are inaccurate and worth correcting for the record:

- *"start.md presents skills and AGENTS.md as a generic feature without flagging this incompatibility."* `apps/www/src/pages/start.md.ts` doesn't mention skills or `AGENTS.md` at all.
- *"AGENTS.md is silently absent. No warning at runtime."* True in isolation, but `AGENTS.md` is optional \u2014 not having one is fine. Most agents don't need one. A warning would nag users who deliberately ran without one.

The real bug, distilled, was: (a) the error message didn't help users diagnose the empty-sandbox case, and (b) the docs section led with the example before flagging that the default empty sandbox starts with no files. Both are now addressed.

## Related

- #21 (Dockerfile example is non-functional) tracked separately as a docs-only fix. Not the same issue \u2014 narrow, self-contained, can ship independently.

> Continuing the structured testing pass. This comment is from Claude Opus 4.7 running in OpenCode. Maintainer asked me to dig into root cause; here's what I found.

## TL;DR

This is **two compounding bugs**:

1. **Primary bug (Flue):** `packages/sdk/src/dev.ts` calls `wrangler.unstable_startWorker(...)` without passing `dev.containerBuildId`. Wrangler's `unstable_startWorker` doesn't default it (only the wrangler CLI path does, via `generateContainerBuildId()`). When `containers[]` is in the config, wrangler's `LocalRuntimeController#onBundleComplete` calls `buildMiniflareOptions` → `getImageNameFromDOClassName(...)` → `assert(options.containerBuildId)` → **fails**. The error is caught and emitted via the controller's error event.

2. **Secondary bug (Flue):** `dev.ts` passes `logLevel: 'info'` to wrangler. Wrangler's logger uses level numbers `error=0, warn=1, info=2, log=3, debug=4` and shows messages where `loggerLevel >= messageLevel`. So at `info`(2), all `logger.log(...)` and `logger.debug(...)` calls are silenced. **Wrangler's central `DevEnv` error handler routes controller errors to `logger.debug(...)` only.** So the assertion above is silently swallowed. The `ProxyController` (which gates all traffic through `pause`/`play` messages) never receives `reloadComplete`, stays paused forever, and every request hangs — including `GET /health`.

End result: Flue prints `Ready on http://localhost:3583`, then nothing. Every request, including `/health`, hangs forever.

## Empirical confirmation

I ran `flue dev --target cloudflare` with `WRANGLER_LOG=debug` set as env, which routes wrangler's logger to a file (`~/Library/Preferences/.wrangler/logs/wrangler-*.log`) at debug level. Output (full stack):

```
--- 2026-05-02T04:35:38.689Z debug
Error in LocalRuntimeController: Error reloading local server
 AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Build ID should be set if containers are defined and enabled
    at getImageNameFromDOClassName (.../wrangler-dist/cli.js:65358:28)
    at .../wrangler-dist/cli.js:65238:90
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at buildMiniflareBindingOptions (.../wrangler-dist/cli.js:65230:22)
    at buildMiniflareOptions (.../wrangler-dist/cli.js:65305:47)
    at process.processTicksAndRejections (node:internal/process/task_queues:103:5)
    at async #onBundleComplete (.../wrangler-dist/cli.js:318195:27)
    at async Mutex.runWith (.../miniflare/dist/src/index.js:58131:48)
```

The relevant wrangler source, in the embedded `cli.js`:

```js
// packages/wrangler/src/api/startDevWorker/utils.ts (around line 315485):
enableContainers: input.dev?.enableContainers ?? config.dev.enable_containers,  // defaults to true
containerBuildId: input.dev?.containerBuildId,                                   // NO default!
```

```js
// packages/wrangler/src/dev/getDevCompatibilityDate.ts (around line 321317):
// (CLI path only; not in unstable_startWorker)
containerBuildId: generateContainerBuildId(),
```

```js
// packages/wrangler/src/dev/miniflare.ts getImageNameFromDOClassName (around line 65358):
function getImageNameFromDOClassName(options) {
  assert(
    options.containerBuildId,
    "Build ID should be set if containers are defined and enabled"
  );
  ...
}
```

So the assertion fires deterministically the first time `onBundleComplete` runs whenever `containers[].length > 0` and `unstable_startWorker` was called without a containerBuildId.

## Why the proxy stays paused (mechanism for "every request hangs, including /health")

`ProxyController` listens for `reloadStart` (→ pause) / `reloadComplete` (→ play) events from runtime controllers:

```js
// packages/wrangler/src/api/startDevWorker/ProxyController.ts (around 316559-316580):
onReloadStart(data) { void this.sendMessageToProxyWorker({ type: "pause" }); }
onReloadComplete(data) {
  this.localServerReady.resolve();
  this.latestConfig = data.config;
  this.latestBundle = data.bundle;
  void this.sendMessageToProxyWorker({ type: "play", proxyData: data.proxyData });
}
```

Because the assertion throws *before* `emitReloadCompleteEvent` fires, the proxy never gets `play`, and every request — including `/health` — is held in pause indefinitely.

Meanwhile, `worker.url` resolves on `proxyController.ready`, which fires once the *proxy worker itself* is up (not the user worker). That's why Flue prints "Server: http://localhost:3583" while requests still hang. The proxy is up; it's just paused.

## The silent-error half

`unstable_DevEnv` dispatches errors as:

```js
// packages/wrangler/src/api/startDevWorker/DevEnv.ts (around line 317574):
this.on("error", (event) => {
  logger.debug(`Error in ${event.source}: ${event.reason}\n`, event.cause);
  logger.debug("=> Error contextual data:", event.data);
});
```

`logger.debug(...)` is only emitted at `loggerLevel === debug`. Flue passes `'info'`, so all controller errors are silently swallowed.

Combined with the assertion above, this is what produces the user-facing symptom: **no error, no progress, total silence after "Ready on..."**.

## Verification: a one-line patch in node_modules unblocks everything

I edited `node_modules/@flue/sdk/dist/index.mjs`'s `unstable_startWorker` call to pass a `containerBuildId`:

```js
this.worker = await this.wrangler.unstable_startWorker({
  config: this.configPath,
  envFiles: this.envFiles,
  build: { nodejsCompatMode: "v2" },
  dev: {
    server: { hostname: "localhost", port: this.port },
    watch: false,
    logLevel: "info",
    containerBuildId: crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 8)  // <-- the fix
  }
});
```

(Format matches `generateContainerBuildId` in wrangler — 8-char UUID slice.)

After the patch:

```bash
$ curl http://localhost:3583/health
{"status":"ok"}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3583/agents/hello/x -d '{"name":"World"}'
{"result":{"greeting":"Hello, World — ..."}}
```

**Single-line fix unblocks the dev server.** All routes work normally with a `containers[]`-bound config.

## Bonus repro: Docker not running — same silent-hang symptom from a different cause

While I had this set up, I also tested what happens when Docker isn't running (`colima stop`). With the `containerBuildId` patch applied (so the assertion no longer fires), wrangler reaches `prepareContainerImagesForDev` → `verifyDockerInstalled`, which throws a *very useful* `UserError`:

```
UserError: The Docker CLI could not be launched. Please ensure that the Docker CLI is
installed and the daemon is running. ... To suppress this error if you do not intend
on triggering any container instances, set dev.enable_containers to false in your
Wrangler config or passing in --enable-containers=false.
```

…which is then **silenced by the same `logLevel: 'info'`** — same `DevEnv.on('error', ...) → logger.debug(...)` path. Same wedge symptom for the user.

So even after fixing #1, #2 still bites whenever Docker isn't running. Both bugs need addressing.

## Proposed fixes (ranked, recommend A+B+C+D, treat E as enhancement)

### A. Pass `containerBuildId` to `unstable_startWorker` (one-line fix; required to unblock at all)

```diff
 dev: {
   server: { hostname: 'localhost', port: this.port },
   watch: false,
   logLevel: 'info',
+  // Wrangler's unstable_startWorker doesn't default containerBuildId; without
+  // this, onBundleComplete crashes whenever containers[] is in the config.
+  containerBuildId: crypto.randomUUID().slice(0, 8),
 },
```

This is mandatory; everything else is improving DX around it.

### B. Bump `logLevel` from `'info'` to `'log'` (or expose a `--debug` flag)

At `'log'` (level 3), users see:
- `⎔ Preparing container image(s)...` / `⎔ Container image(s) ready` — explains the multi-second wait.
- `⎔ Starting local server...` — explains why `/health` doesn't immediately respond.

At `'info'` (current), all of these are hidden. Bumping to `'log'` is one-character; would have made #22 self-diagnosing.

### C. Surface `DevEnv` errors at user-visible level

Wrangler's own central error handler swallows controller errors at `logger.debug(...)`. There are two ways for Flue to fix this:

1. Set `logLevel: 'debug'` (noisy, but errors will surface).
2. Subscribe to wrangler's events directly. `unstable_DevEnv` extends `EventEmitter`. If `unstable_startWorker` returns a handle that can listen on `'error'`, Flue can re-emit those errors to its own console at user-visible level. (Worth checking whether the API exposes this — the worker handle returned by `createWorkerObject` doesn't seem to, but `devEnv` does internally.)

If neither is feasible, at minimum (B) above plus a Flue-level pre-flight check: detect `containers[]` in the merged wrangler config and run `docker info` (or equivalent) before calling `unstable_startWorker`. If Docker is unavailable, fail fast with a clear `[flue]` error pointing at the `enable_containers: false` workaround. Cheap and catches the most common "no docker" case before wrangler swallows it.

### D. Add `--no-containers` flag to `flue dev`

```bash
npx flue dev --target cloudflare --no-containers
```

…which passes `dev.enableContainers: false` (and removes `containers[]` from the merged dev config?) so users can iterate on non-container agents in a project that also has containers without paying the Docker startup cost. Useful for CI smoke tests too.

### E. Use `setOptions` for reloads instead of `disposeWorker` + `startWorker`

Currently Flue's `reload()` does:

```js
async reload(buildChanged) {
  if (!buildChanged) return;
  await this.disposeWorker();
  await this.startWorker();  // <-- regenerates containerBuildId
}
```

Each `startWorker()` (with my fix) generates a fresh `containerBuildId`, which then mismatches `#currentContainerBuildId` in wrangler's `LocalRuntimeController`, triggering `prepareContainerImagesForDev` again. So **every wrangler.jsonc edit (or new agent file) re-runs container prep**, even if the Dockerfile is byte-identical.

If `unstable_startWorker` returns a worker with a `setConfig`/`setOptions` API (or if `unstable_DevEnv` is reusable across reloads), use that instead of disposing + recreating. Big DX win for projects with containers — saves multi-second container prep on every save.

This is more invasive than A-D; treat as an enhancement.

**Root cause update:** The model registry mutation approach (patching `getModel()` result's `baseUrl`/`headers`) does not work in Flue's bundled server because of esbuild module duplication. The bundle contains two inlined copies of `@mariozechner/pi-ai` — one resolved from the project root (used by the agent code), one resolved through `@flue/sdk`'s dependency chain (used by `pi-agent-core`'s call path). Both have separate `modelRegistry` Maps and separate Anthropic client constructors. Evidence: `streamSimpleAnthropic` and `streamSimpleAnthropic2` coexist in `dist/server.mjs`; the `api.anthropic.com` URL appears on the wire despite `model.baseUrl` reading correctly in the agent scope.

**Working workaround:** Patch `globalThis.fetch` at module init to rewrite outgoing Anthropic URLs and inject custom headers. `globalThis` is a true singleton regardless of bundle structure.

**Correct fix (from the framework side):** Mark `@mariozechner/pi-ai` as `external` in Flue's esbuild config, or expose a `providers` option on `init()` that configures the Anthropic client directly rather than relying on the model registry.

thinking about this from the managed-agent / control-plane angle: the missing primitive feels like `Run`.

`Session` is durable conversation state. `Run` is one execution attempt against that session: prompt, skill, task, webhook, SSE request, etc. Once that exists, cancellation gets much cleaner and does not need to be modeled as deleting or mutating the session itself.

possible small shape:

- terminal event is `run_end { runId, status: "completed" | "failed" | "cancelled" }`
- local API can start with standard `AbortSignal`

- session history stays intact; cancelled runs become observable attempts, not deleted sessions

> What is possible with the tool broker that isn't possible today?

For Part 1 alone, every case has a workaround — the argument is *shape*. Gating, discovery, and lifecycle of tool sources are all the same kind of problem; one primitive captures them more cleanly than N scattered patches. A couple become load-bearing once Part 2 lands.

> `// list tools across all three sources uniformly` — what does this accomplish?

Today: debug / introspection. In code mode it's load-bearing — the model writes against a generated TS surface, so with many providers attached it needs `tools.search('send email')` to discover candidates rather than ship every schema every turn. Also gives runtime created or registered tools (skills, dynamically discovered MCP) somewhere to live.

> opt-in per-prompt is more common; no-op overrides handle the rest

Agreed, opt-in stays in the API. Pattern block earns its keep with carve-outs:

- read-only prompts (block `*delete*` / `*write*` against a trusted GitHub MCP)
- low-trust user input (default-deny or in future, escalate destructive ops)
- phased agents (planning = read-only, execution = full)
- MCP servers that add tools post-hoc — opt-in lists silently drop new ones; patterns keep coverage

No-op overrides work surgically, but require knowing every tool name up front + writing N stubs + repeating per-prompt-site — vs. one regex. Blocked tools should also disappear from the catalog the model sees, not just be rejected on dispatch.

> rotate a token without rebuilding the connection — give an example?

Anywhere a short-lived token outlives a session:

- **AWS STS** — 1h default, 12h max
- **GitHub Actions OIDC** — per-job, ≤1h
- **SSO / SAML** refresh, **multi-tenant** per-request tokens

Today the bearer header is captured into `requestInit` at construction time (`mcp.ts:25-55`); rotation = `close()` + reconnect + rewire `tools: [...]` + restart holders. Secret-by-reference collapses it to `secrets.set(...)`. If long-lived agents with short-lived creds aren't a Flue target yet, deprioritize.

@davidmyriel — sketching this out as a fellow contributor in case it helps the maintainers shape the work.

**One-line proposal.** Mirror the existing `getVirtualSandbox` shape (factory return, lazy peer dep, `MountableFs(InMemoryFs)` mounted at `/workspace`) with a pure object-store storage model — no sidecar SQLite, no external metadata DB.

### The three substantive choices

| Choice | What | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Pure object-store + key conventions + `CopyObject` for `mv`/`cp` | Zero new infra; bucket *is* the source of truth; works on every S3-compatible backend in scope (AWS, Tigris, MinIO, R2-S3-API, GCS-XML). |
| Metadata | Per-object headers (`x-amz-meta-flue-type`, `flue-mode`) + in-process LRU caches (stat 60 s, list 30 s, negative 5 s) | Stateless. No schema, no migrations, no recovery procedure. Process restart is free. |
| Client surface | User passes their own `S3Client` instance | Mirrors `getVirtualSandbox(bucket: R2Bucket)` — instance, not config. flue stays out of credentials and out of provider-config drift. |

Other details (peer-dep wiring, package layout, symlink encoding, empty-dir markers, conditional-write strategy, multipart thresholds) all follow from these three.

### API sketch

```ts
export interface S3SandboxOptions {
  bucket: string;
  prefix?: string;                    // session isolation; default 'default'
  metadataMode?: 'auto' | 'sidecar';  // 'auto' = headers (v1); 'sidecar' = ENOTSUP in v1
  maxEntries?: number;                // readdir cap, default 10_000
  statTtlMs?: number;                 // default 60_000
  listTtlMs?: number;                 // default 30_000
  multipartThreshold?: number;        // default 5 * 1024 * 1024
}

export async function getS3Sandbox(): Promise<BashFactory>;
export async function getS3Sandbox(client: S3Client, options: S3SandboxOptions): Promise<BashFactory>;
```

`@aws-sdk/client-s3` lives in `peerDependenciesMeta.optional`, lazy-imported, so users who never touch the s3 path pay nothing — same pattern as `wrangler` today.

### Four PRs to land it

1. `S3FileSystem` adapter against the just-bash FS contract (read/write/stat/lstat/mkdir/readdir/rm/cp/mv/symlink/readlink/realpath). Mocked-S3 unit tests.
2. Caching + symlink resolver (depth cap 40 = POSIX `SYMLOOP_MAX`).
3. `getS3Sandbox` entry, package wiring (`./s3` export, peer dep), example agent.
4. MinIO via testcontainers in CI; parity test against the existing CF path; `connectors/sandbox--s3.md` + `docs/connect-s3.md` worked examples.

### Trade-offs being accepted (would go in the connector doc)

- `mv` is `CopyObject + DeleteObject` — server-side copy, no re-upload, but not atomic.
- `link()` is `CopyObject` — no shared inode, no refcount. Same compromise `s3fs-fuse` makes.
- `appendFile` is GET → concat → PUT — not atomic.
- Sub-second mtime is lost (S3 `LastModified` is second-resolution).
- Concurrent writers across processes are last-writer-wins in v1. Conditional writes (`If-Match`) are the v2 unlock — S3 supports them since Aug 2024 and R2/Tigris/MinIO match.

### Real open questions for maintainers

1. **`link()` semantics.** `CopyObject` with documented divergence, or throw `ENOTSUP`? Both are defensible.
2. **Empty-args overload** parity with the CF module — should `@flue/sdk/s3` also return an `InMemoryFs`-backed factory when called with no arguments, or only the bucket-backed shape?
3. **Bundle target verification.** The issue mentions Workers without an R2 binding. AWS SDK v3 has had a Workers-friendly fetch handler since 3.582; needs a Phase 3 verification step against a `tsdown`-built bundle.

### Out of v1, deliberately

Sidecar SQLite, external SQL metadata, cross-bucket `mv`, customer-managed encryption. The `metadataMode: 'sidecar'` option name is reserved so v2 stays API-compatible.

### Offer

Architecture decisions. Four calls I had to make; each is one line away
from the alternative if you'd prefer differently.

---

**1. Where does `usage` surface?**

- **Option A**: only on `turn_end` events. Granular, consistent with the
  existing event model.
- **Option B**: only on `PromptResponse`. Simple for script-style agents,
  but loses per-turn detail in tool-use loops.
- **Option C (chosen)**: both. `turn_end` for granularity, `PromptResponse`
  for the common aggregate case. Ignorable if you only want one.

**Why C**: the two answer different questions ("what did this specific
turn cost?" vs. "what did this whole call cost?") and computing either
from the other forces the consumer to add state. Both are cheap, both
are additive.

**Open**: if you'd rather pick A or B, removing the other is a handful
of lines. C was my default because neither surface alone covered the
obvious use cases.

---

**2. Schema-callers**

`session.prompt(text, { result: schema })` returns `InferOutput<S>`
directly. Three options:

- **Option A (chosen)**: leave it untouched. Schema-callers read usage
  from `turn_end` events.
- **Option B**: wrap the return as `{ value, usage }`. Cleanest API, but
  a breaking change.
- **Option C**: attach `usage` as a hidden property on the return
  object. Breaks TypeScript's shape contract.

**Why A**: B is breaking, C is a footgun. Current behavior stays
identical for schema-callers; they opt into usage via events.

**Open**: if you want B in a future major, this PR is forward-compatible
with it.

---

**3. Compaction cost rollup**

Compaction runs 1–2 internal summarization calls when context grows.
Options:

- **Option A (chosen)**: expose on `compaction_end`, don't merge into
  the in-flight `PromptResponse.usage`.
- **Option B**: merge into the caller's aggregate. "Total cost of this
  prompt" becomes truly total.
- **Option C**: suppress entirely (pre-PR behavior).

**Why A**: compaction is agent-config-driven maintenance, not user
work. Rolling it into `PromptResponse.usage` conflates "what did my
prompt cost" with "what did the agent's housekeeping cost this time".
Surfacing it separately lets consumers choose. `compaction_end` is the
natural home.

**Open**: if you want B (rollup), the change is in `session.ts` where
the compaction listener currently only emits; it would also add into
the active `currentCallUsage` accumulator. Easy.

---

**4. Task-child rollup**

`session.task()` spawns a child session. Events already carry
`parentSessionId` / `taskId`, so consumers can aggregate. Options:

- **Option A (chosen)**: no built-in rollup. Each task emits its own
  `turn_end` events; consumers that want parent-scoped totals group by
  `parentSessionId`.
- **Option B**: sum child cost into the parent's `PromptResponse.usage`
  automatically.
- **Option C**: expose a new `task_end.usage` field aggregating the
  child's total.

**Why A**: B forces one aggregation policy (include children → total
goes up unexpectedly for callers that didn't spawn tasks directly).
C is defensible but adds surface area.

**Open**: C is a small add if you want it — `task_end` is already
emitted, and the child session is tracked in `activeTasks`. I can
include it in this PR if you prefer.

---

**Other small calls**:

- `ModelInfo` is `{ provider, id }` rather than the full pi-ai `Model`
  (which has cost tables, headers, compat flags). Smaller public surface,
  no risk of consumers depending on pi-ai internals.
- `Usage` is re-exported from pi-ai so consumers don't need a direct
  dependency to type their callbacks. Happy to revisit if you'd rather
  define a Flue-owned subset.
- No new public event-subscription API (`agent.onEvent(...)`). The
  existing channel goes through `FlueContextInternal.setEventCallback`
  which the webhook runtime consumes for SSE. Adding a public subscribe
  is a bigger discussion — out of scope here.

Happy to iterate on any of these.

Closing this — Standard Schema's validation interface is supported by both valibot and zod today, but **JSON Schema generation is not**, and that's a hard requirement for Flue's structured-output flow (we embed a JSON Schema in the prompt to tell the model what shape to return).

There are two separate specs in the Standard Schema family:

- **`StandardSchemaV1`** — the validation interface (`~standard.validate`). Implemented by valibot, zod, arktype, etc.
- **`StandardJSONSchemaV1`** — a separate, optional spec that adds a `~standard.jsonSchema` converter (`{ input(opts), output(opts) }`) for emitting JSON Schema in a vendor-agnostic way.

The confusion: zod 4 ships `z.toJSONSchema(schema)` and valibot ships `@valibot/to-json-schema` — so people quite reasonably say these libs "support JSON Schema out of the box." They do, but only through library-specific imports that consume internal state. Neither library exposes anything on `~standard.jsonSchema`.

Verified directly against the v4.2.0 tag — `packages/zod/src/v4/core/schemas.ts` initializes `~standard` with only:

```ts
inst["~standard"] = {
  validate: (value) => { ... },
  vendor: "zod",
  version: 1 as const,
};
```

Same story in valibot 1.4 (`library/src/types/standard.ts`): `version`, `vendor`, `validate`, `types`. No `jsonSchema`.

So today, requiring `StandardJSONSchemaV1` would reject **every** real schema users would bring, including the valibot we already document. We'd be shipping a contract no library satisfies.

We'll revisit when major libs adopt `StandardJSONSchemaV1` on `~standard`. Until then, valibot stays the canonical path. If/when zod, valibot, etc. expose `~standard.jsonSchema` natively, the migration becomes trivial and we'll do it.

We took a slightly different path than provider-native structured outputs: instead, the SDK now injects two internal tools — `finish` and `give_up` — for the duration of any `.prompt()` / `.skill()` / `.task()` call that has a `result` schema. The LLM submits its final answer as `finish` tool arguments, which means:

- The schema travels with the tool definition (the canonical channel every provider already understands), not as prompt-text instructions.
- pi-agent-core validates `finish`'s args against the JSON Schema before `execute` is called.
- Inside `execute`, valibot does the final round of validation and returns the parsed output (transforms, defaults, refinements). On failure it throws — pi-agent-core surfaces that as a tool-error to the LLM, which can self-correct on the next turn.
- A successful call sets `terminate: true` to end the loop naturally.
- `give_up` lets the model signal "I cannot determine the answer," which surfaces to the user as a typed `ResultUnavailableError`.

The marker-based extraction (`---RESULT_START---` / `---RESULT_END---`) and its regex parser are gone. Public API surface (`PromptResultResponse`, `result` option, etc.) is unchanged.

Tool-calling is universally supported across the providers Flue targets (Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare Workers AI, etc.), so this works without per-provider branching. Native structured-output APIs may still be worth layering in later as an optimization, but the correctness gap that motivated this issue is closed.

Good question — landed on this while researching the provider surface for an unrelated discussion. Sharing what I found so the answer is on the record.

## Short answer

Not today via `init({ model })`, but the gap is small.

## What I checked

**Runtime side (pi-ai):** Flue's model runtime (`@mariozechner/pi-ai`) explicitly supports Ollama through the "Any OpenAI-compatible API" path. Recipe is a hand-built `Model<'openai-completions'>` object pointed at `http://localhost:11434/v1`, passed to pi-ai's `stream()` directly. Documented in `@mariozechner/pi-ai` README under *Custom Models*.

**SDK side (Flue):** Model config is a string only.

```ts
// packages/sdk/src/types.ts:196
export type ModelConfig = string | false;
```

`resolveModel()` parses `'provider/model-id'` and dispatches to `getModel(provider, modelId)` from pi-ai (`packages/sdk/src/internal.ts:46-91`). pi-ai has no Ollama models in its built-in registry, so `'ollama/llama-3.1-8b'` throws:

```
[flue] Unknown model "ollama/llama-3.1-8b". Provider "ollama" / model id "llama-3.1-8b" is not registered with @mariozechner/pi-ai.
```

`ProviderSettings.baseUrl` does exist on the public surface (`types.ts:147-164`), but `applyProviderSettings()` only overrides `baseUrl`/`headers`/`apiKey` on an *already-resolved* model. It cannot introduce a new `ollama` provider key from nothing — pi-ai's registry is the one that decides which provider strings resolve.

## Workaround possible today

Bypass `init({ model })` and call pi-ai directly inside a handler with a hand-built `Model<'openai-completions'>`. Works, but skips Flue's role and `ProviderSettings` plumbing, so it loses some of the reason you'd reach for Flue.

## What a real fix looks like

Two clean shapes, both small:

1. Accept a `Model<Api>` object as `ModelConfig` alongside the string. User wires the Ollama model object themselves, Flue passes it straight through to pi-ai. No new provider registration needed.
2. Add a `customModels` registry on `init()` keyed by `'provider/id'`. Flue's resolver checks the registry before calling `getModel`. Slightly more ergonomic for `flue.config.ts` reuse.

Either lets the same `Model` shape flow that pi-ai already documents for Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, etc.

i took a pass through current `virtual-sandbox.ts` + the `@cloudflare/shell` implementation, and i think this explains the behavior.

`getVirtualSandbox(env.KNOWLEDGE_BASE)` is not really mounting raw R2 object keys today. it builds an `@cloudflare/shell` `Workspace`:

```ts
const ws = new Workspace({
  sql: storage.sql,
  r2: bucket,
  name: () => prefix,
});
```

that `Workspace` uses DO SQLite as the filesystem index. R2 is only the blob backend for files the Workspace itself writes/spills. `readDir()` / `exists()` query the SQL table, not `bucket.list()`, so objects uploaded directly with `wrangler r2 object put articles/foo.md` have no corresponding `/articles/foo.md` row and stay invisible.

so i think the report is valid from a DX/docs perspective, but there are probably two different concepts getting collapsed:

1. durable virtual workspace: DO SQLite index + optional R2 blob storage
2. direct object-store mount: bucket keys are the filesystem

the README currently sounds like (2), while the code implements (1).

## Review findings

1. **React hook-order violation:** `useFlueOperation()` conditionally calls `use()`. Rendering `null` and later an operation changes the hook count and can crash React (`packages/react/src/index.tsx:176-182`).
2. **`stop()` does not stop the agent:** it only aborts the browser request/stream; an admitted server submission continues running and mutating history (`packages/client/src/index.ts:416-425`, `packages/runtime/src/node/agent-coordinator.ts:433-445`).
3. **History remains incomplete:** prior user prompts are not emitted into the durable stream. Optimistic messages only exist in the browser that submitted them, so replay elsewhere reconstructs assistant output without user messages (`packages/client/src/index.ts:616-629`, `packages/runtime/src/session.ts:2058-2070`).
4. **Reconnect can strand operations:** calling `connect()`/`reconnect()` while streaming replaces the associated stream without carrying its active operation; its promise and queued sends can remain pending forever (`packages/client/src/index.ts:393-399`, `501-595`).
5. **Provider-level custom `fetch` is ignored:** app options expose it, but `mergeControllerOptions()` omits it. This affects React, Vue, and Svelte auth/polyfill use (`packages/client/src/index.ts:687-701`).
6. **Svelte prematurely disposes controllers:** dropping the store’s subscriber count to zero releases the shared controller even before component destruction, breaking later resubscription (`packages/svelte/src/index.ts:62-70`).

The original report focuses on `flue_session_entries.data`, but we found two other SQLite/Durable Object write paths that can still hit the same per-cell limit even after session text is chunked:

1. `packages/runtime/src/runtime/stream-chunks.ts`
   - `StreamChunkWriter.flush()` currently writes `JSON.stringify(events)` as one `appendStreamChunkSegment(...)` body.
   - If a throttled flush contains a large `text_delta` / `thinking_delta` / similar event batch, the stream segment body itself can exceed the SQLite value limit.

2. `packages/runtime/src/runtime/event-stream-store.ts`
   - `SqliteEventStreamStore.appendEvent()` writes `JSON.stringify(event)` directly into `flue_event_stream_entries.data`.
   - Final or replay events such as a large `message_end` can exceed the limit even when the session-entry store has chunked equivalent content.

In our app-side patch, the deterministic fix had to cover all three lanes:

- session entry text/thinking blocks, using the existing image-chunk style side table and transparent hydration;
- throttled stream chunk segments, by splitting large delta events/batches before `appendStreamChunkSegment`;
- SQLite event stream entries, by adding a side table for oversized event JSON and hydrating in `readEvents`.

We also had to ensure the Cloudflare/Vite optimized runtime chunk was patched, because `SqliteEventStreamStore` can be bundled into the Vite `flue-app-*.js` optimized dependency rather than only appearing in `@flue/runtime/dist/handle-agent-*.mjs`.

So I think the upstream fix for this issue should audit all SQLite text/blob cells that can receive model/tool/event payloads, not only `flue_session_entries.data`.

Tracked this down — root cause is in `@flue/sdk`'s `HttpClient`, and it looks **already fixed on `main`** (just not yet published).

**Cause (beta.7):** `HttpClient` stores the global `fetch` unbound and then calls it as a method:

```ts
// packages/sdk/src/http.ts (beta.7)
this.fetchImpl = options.fetch ?? fetch          // detached reference
// ...
return this.fetchImpl(input, { ... })            // called as this.fetchImpl(...)
```

In the browser, calling a detached `fetch` as a method throws `TypeError: Illegal invocation` (Node/undici doesn't enforce the receiver, which is why it works there). `@durable-streams/client`'s `createFetchWithBackoff` treats that `TypeError` as a retryable error and retries with `maxRetries: Infinity`, so the request never resolves — the stream sits forever with no events, no error, and (since the throw happens before the request is sent) no network activity. That's the "hangs in browser, works in Node" behavior.

**Already fixed on `main`:** commit `71f856a4` changed it to

```ts
this.fetchImpl = options.fetch ?? fetch.bind(globalThis);
```

with a comment describing exactly this. `main`'s `package.json` still reads `1.0.0-beta.7`, so the fix doesn't appear to be on npm yet — a release would resolve this.

**Workaround on beta.7** (confirmed against the repro): pass a bound fetch to `createFlueClient`:

```ts
createFlueClient({ baseUrl, fetch: globalThis.fetch.bind(globalThis) })
```

With the default client → `events=0` (hangs); with the bound fetch → `events=100`.

(Possible hardening on the `@durable-streams/client` side: not retrying a synchronous `TypeError` from the fetch fn as if it were a transient network failure would surface this immediately instead of hanging.)

## Findings: migrating off `/compat` to the modern pi-ai API

Context: we're currently on `@earendil-works/pi-ai` / `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core` `0.80.2` but routed almost everything through the `@earendil-works/pi-ai/compat` entrypoint to get the upgrade working. The goal was to move onto pi's newer, opt-in provider API and ship a lighter bundle (only the providers we use, ~2MB less JS).

### What the new pi-ai API looks like
The modern surface (already shipped in pi-ai) is `createModels()` + per-provider factory imports:

```ts
import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai";
import { anthropicProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/anthropic";

const models = createModels();
models.setProvider(anthropicProvider());
```

`@earendil-works/pi-ai` (root) is core-only and pulls **no** catalogs or SDK impls; `providers/<id>` pulls just that provider; `providers/all` pulls everything. The README's migration table maps every compat symbol we use (`getModel`/`getModels` → `models.getModel()`, `stream`/`streamSimple` → `models.stream()`, `registerApiProvider` → `createProvider()` + `models.setProvider()`, `registerFauxProvider` → `fauxProvider()`).

### The blocker for the bundle win
The selective-provider entrypoint from the original PR (`@earendil-works/pi-agent-core/base`, added in 0.79.8) was **removed in 0.80.0** in favor of an explicit `Models` instance. But that refactor only re-plumbed the **harness** (`AgentHarnessOptions.models`). The low-level `Agent` / `agent-loop` that flue actually uses still statically imports `streamSimple` from `/compat`:

- `pi-agent-core/dist/agent.js` → `import { streamSimple } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/compat"`
- `pi-agent-core/dist/agent-loop.js` → `import { EventStream, streamSimple, validateToolArguments } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/compat"`

And `compat.js` eagerly constructs the full provider set at module-eval (`const compatModels = builtinModels()`), with `compat.js` marked in pi-ai's `sideEffects`. Since flue imports `{ Agent }` from pi-agent-core, the compat module — and therefore all ~35 providers + catalogs — is unavoidably in the graph today. Both pi-agent-core entrypoints (`.` and `./node`) re-export `agent.js`, so there's no entrypoint that avoids it.

**Net:** migrating flue's own runtime off `/compat` is necessary but **not sufficient**. The bundle stays large until pi-agent-core also stops importing compat.

### This is a known, temporary phase upstream
Per Mario (pi author), compat is an intentional transitional shim. The pi-ai README states: *"Avoid `@earendil-works/pi-ai/compat` in new bundled apps … It will be removed in a future release."* And he's explicitly called out the agent package as the remaining work: *"the CHANGELOG will be updated with a migration guide once the remaining work (coding agent and new agent harness integration) is complete sometime later this week."*

The required upstream fix is small: source `EventStream`/`validateToolArguments` from the pi-ai root and drop (or lazy-load) the compat `streamSimple` default in `Agent`/`agent-loop` (flue always passes its own `streamFn`, so that default is dead weight for us).

### Recommendation / next steps
- Hold off on a user-facing flue config change (e.g. `providers: [...]`) — not worth committing to an API surface before the upstream pieces land.
- The flue-side `/compat` → `createModels()` migration is forward-compatible and can be done independently when we choose, but on its own it won't shrink the deployment.
- Gate the actual bundle-size win on pi-agent-core dropping its compat import (Mario's imminent release, or a small upstream PR).

Thanks for the detailed write-up. I dug into how tool schemas flow through the runtime to see how much of this is already possible and how much is a genuine gap. Findings below, with a recommendation to move most of this to a discussion.

## One correction on the framing

The JSON Schema isn't memoized "at tool-registration time" in a way that locks the shape. `valibotToJsonSchema` is a pure conversion cache keyed by the schema's object identity (a `WeakMap`): a *different* schema instance always produces a *fresh* JSON Schema. So the cache never prevents narrowing — it just avoids re-converting the same schema object.

## What already works today: per-call schemas

`session.prompt()` / `skill()` / `task()` already accept a per-call `tools` array (`OperationOptions.tools`), and it's threaded all the way to the provider: `runPromptCall` → `withCallOverrides` swaps the entire tool set for the duration of the call, `assembleModelTools` rebuilds it, and `createCustomTools` runs `valibotToJsonSchema(tool.input)` on whatever you pass.

That means if you build a fresh Valibot schema from runtime state and pass it in, the model **does** see the narrowed schema:

```ts
const candidates = await prepareCandidates();
await session.prompt("Pick one", {
  tools: [defineTool({
    name: "choose",
    description: "...",
    input: v.object({ id: v.picklist(candidates.map(c => c.id)) }),
    run: ({ input }) => ...,
  })],
});
```

For the **stage-machine** case where each stage is its own operation (natural when a workflow orchestrates the stages), this fully covers the ask — no permissive schema + revalidation workaround needed.

## What genuinely doesn't work: mid-loop narrowing

The gap is narrowing the schema **between turns within a single agent loop**. Today `withCallOverrides` fixes the tool set for the whole multi-turn completion; there's no per-turn hook to re-narrow as state evolves inside one `prompt()`.

Good news on feasibility: the underlying loop (pi-agent-core) already has a per-turn `prepareNextTurn` hook whose returned context can carry a different `tools` array, so this is buildable inside the runtime rather than requiring an upstream change. The real cost is API design (how a tool expresses "recompute my input schema from current state") plus making mid-loop tool swaps deterministic for durability/replay — not a small, self-contained patch.

## Constrained decoding

This one is a larger, upstream-dependent effort. The provider layer only exposes a per-provider capability flag; the tool type sent to providers doesn't currently carry a `strict`/structured-output field, so wiring true constrained decoding would need changes across the provider layer, the loop's tool type, and the runtime. It also solves a different problem than a runtime-derived candidate list (strict mode enforces a *fixed* schema, not a dynamically computed one).

Worth noting the leading SDKs land in the same place: the pattern there is a static schema + validation/repair loop (which this runtime already has), with per-step variation limited to selecting a subset of already-declared tools and swapping descriptions — not injecting new schemas mid-loop.

## Suggestion

I'd propose splitting this:

1. **Per-call dynamic schemas** already work — happy to add a docs example if that unblocks the stage-machine use case.
2. **Mid-loop per-turn narrowing** and **constrained decoding** are real feature requests but need design (durability/replay, public API surface, upstream provider work). These fit better as a discussion where we can weigh the API shape and the replay implications.

If that split sounds right, this issue can move to a discussion for (2) and (3).

Thanks for filing this — the underlying pain here was real, but investigating it led us to a different (and better) fix than a direct settlement-read API, and it ended up clarifying a piece of Flue's model that we want to record here.

## Why we didn't build a settlement-by-id API

Taken literally, this issue asks for job semantics on a dispatched input: "recover submission X's terminal outcome by id." But `dispatch()` delivers input into an agent's *living conversation* — it's not a job with a single result. An agent can produce zero, one, or many messages in response to a dispatched input, interleaved with other work in the session; there's no clean "the result of dispatch X" to hand back. Building an API around that shape would import request/response semantics into a place they don't belong. Where terminal-outcome-by-id genuinely is the right shape — a unit of work with one result you can poll for — Flue already has that: a **workflow run** (`invoke()` + `client.runs.get(runId)` / `client.runs.stream()`).

We also confirmed the conversation is deliberately the *only* source of truth here — not a projection that happens to be inconvenient to query. A parallel settlement ledger would just drift from the record of what actually happened.

## What we shipped instead

The real, valid complaint was that recovering a dispatched input's outcome from the conversation required a brittle walk — scanning message text and parsing an id out of a message-id string, because dispatch interruptions were flattened into plain `role: 'user'` text bubbles with no structured signal.

That's fixed by #404 (e113c4a6): internal signals (including a dispatched input's abort/interruption advisories) now project as typed `role: 'system'` messages carrying a stable `purpose` (`user` / `assistant` / `dispatch` / `advisory`), a `display` hint, and a structured `signal: { tagName, attributes }` descriptor with `submissionId` preserved. A caller can now filter `history()`/`observe()` messages by `purpose === 'advisory'` and `submissionId` to find a failed/aborted dispatch — no text parsing, no message-id string parsing.

## The broader clarification

Digging into this surfaced that **direct HTTP agent prompts had grown the same category error**: `client.agents.prompt()`, `client.agents.wait()` returning a result, and HTTP `?wait=result` all let an external caller treat a conversational turn as a synchronous call with a return value — the same job-shaped thinking we were rejecting for dispatch, just on the other admission path.

Since this is pre-1.0, we removed that surface rather than build around it (b4978d80, changelog in e9fc1e10):
- `client.agents.prompt()` and `AgentPromptResult`/`AgentPromptResponse` are gone.
- `client.agents.wait()` is now a completion-await: it resolves `void` on success and throws `FlueExecutionError` on failure/abort — it does not return a result.
- HTTP `POST /agents/:name/:id` is fire-and-forget only; `?wait=result` on the agent route now returns `400 invalid_request` with guidance to use `wait()` or observe the stream.
- The durable `submission_settled` record and its wire projections dropped their `result` field (kept `outcome` + `error`).

So the model is now consistent end to end: **every** way of delivering input to an agent — direct HTTP prompt or `dispatch()` — is fire-and-forget, and the conversation (`history()` / `observe()`) is the one place you read what happened, including a dispatched or direct input's failure/abort. If you need an actual request→terminal-result contract, that's what workflows are for.

Closing this as resolved by the above, rather than as originally scoped.

Confirmed — and the diagnosis of the ordering is exactly right: the retry-budget check ran before the recovery branch, so exhaustion (and timeout, and crash-interrupted abort) skipped the repair path entirely and left the parent `task` tool_start with no terminal tool event.

One deliberate divergence from the proposed fix: we don't reattach/resume the child after the budget is spent. Child resume already runs inside normal recovery attempts and consumes the parent's budget by design — exhaustion is the backstop for exactly that resume path crash-looping, and re-running it post-budget would reintroduce unbounded work with nothing bounding it.

What shipped instead (c5e7ef45) makes terminalization itself the guarantee, for all tools rather than just `task`: every terminal settlement (retry exhaustion, timeout, post-input interruption, abort) first settles the conversation to a deterministic rest state. Recorded outcomes are preserved; every unresolved call gets an explicit interrupted-error `tool_outcome` and the batch is committed, so no tool_start ever rests without a terminal tool event. For a `task` call the marker carries the retained child conversation id, and the `child_session_retained` link is untouched — the child transcript stays inspectable. The terminal advisory now carries the interrupted-call list as structured `attributes.interruptedTools` (also on the settlement error's `meta`), so you can settle your run state without parsing text. Conversations already stuck in the dangling state self-heal on their next prompt.

This also fixed something worse than the transcript shape: an unsettled trailing batch was silently dropped from all future model context, so the model never knew the task had run at all. Settled turns now stay visible.

Some additional implementation context:

### Pi already has a partial additions-only path

Pi 0.83.0 defines `AgentToolResult.addedToolNames`. The agent loop copies it into the persisted tool-result message, and supported provider adapters can move those definitions out of the initial top-level prefix and load them at the historical tool-result position:

- Contract: [`types.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb/packages/ai/src/types.ts#L415-L430)
- Agent-loop propagation: [`agent-loop.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb/packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts#L773-L786)
- Deferred classification and fallback: [`deferred-tools.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb/packages/ai/src/utils/deferred-tools.ts#L7-L38)
- Anthropic adapter: [`anthropic-messages.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb/packages/ai/src/api/anthropic-messages.ts#L939-L970)
- OpenAI Responses adapter: [`openai-responses.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb/packages/ai/src/api/openai-responses.ts#L257-L287)

Flue currently does not emit `addedToolNames`, persist it in its canonical tool-outcome records, or reconstruct it during replay, so conditional additions bypass this optimization.

Wiring that field through would help with additions directly caused by a completed tool call, but it would not cover the whole Flue resource lifecycle:

- removal has no marker;
- updating an existing tool's description or schema changes the definition at its earlier load point;
- remove → re-add can reuse an old historical addition marker;
- a tool added because of an external delivery, signal, or initialization change has no causal tool result to annotate; and
- recovery and replay need the transition in durable canonical state, not only in an in-memory Pi message.

### Provider mappings

One provider-neutral representation could be a durable chronological delta such as:

```ts
type ToolAvailabilityDelta = {
  added: ToolDefinition[];
  removed: string[];
  updated: ToolDefinition[];
  allowed?: string[];
};
```

Adapters could then choose the strongest available mapping:

| Capability | Possible mapping |
| --- | --- |
| Anthropic models with mid-conversation tool changes | Stable definition catalog plus `tool_addition` / `tool_removal` blocks |
| Anthropic models with deferred references only | Pi's `addedToolNames` / `defer_loading` path for eligible additions; explicit fallback for removals and updates |
| OpenAI with a finite known catalog | Stable top-level definitions plus per-step `allowed_tools` |
| OpenAI with genuinely late-bound additions | Tool-search output or `additional_tools`, appended at a stable historical point |
| Provider without a suitable native mechanism | Stable dispatcher/meta-tool, or an explicitly documented cache-busting fallback |

Anthropic's current [mid-conversation tool changes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#mid-conversation-tool-changes) are the closest native match for conditional workflow tools, but model support is limited. The docs' Sonnet 4.6 example is not among the supported models.

OpenAI explicitly recommends a stable tool list with [`allowed_tools`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling#tool-choice) when the goal is to vary availability while maximizing cache reuse.

For a provider-neutral precedent, OpenCode's active v2 branch keeps one invariant provider-visible `execute({ code })` tool and moves the changing registry behind it:

- Stable dispatcher: [`codemode/tool.ts`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/6a543791b62d154de50666ec512e4756fcf050d7/packages/core/src/codemode/tool.ts#L22-L58)
- Catalog delta rendering: [`codemode/instructions.ts`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/6a543791b62d154de50666ec512e4756fcf050d7/packages/core/src/codemode/instructions.ts#L41-L140)
- Per-request tool snapshot: [`session/context.ts`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/6a543791b62d154de50666ec512e4756fcf050d7/packages/core/src/session/context.ts#L80-L108)

The important invariant is the same across these approaches: keep the provider-visible prefix stable, append availability changes at their chronological point, and enforce the live registry when a tool is executed.

### Extra cases worth testing

- `A → B` and `B → A`
- zero tools → one tool and one tool → zero tools
- same-name description/schema updates
- remove → re-add
- changes caused by tool results and by external deliveries/signals
- persistence, crash recovery, replay, join/resume, and compaction
- raw serialized provider payloads plus cache-read/cache-write metrics where the provider exposes them

Thanks for the exceptional report — the Logpush timeline made this diagnosable, and you were right on every count: it wasn't app misuse, it wasn't the pre-fix #497 hang, and there was a remaining silent non-settlement path. It's now fixed on main; details below, and instructions for once the next release is out.

**Root cause.** Two compounding defects. First, the durability timeout was only enforced (a) cooperatively between turns and (b) by the coordinator's reconcile pass — and on Cloudflare that pass ran in the same loop that awaited your attempt, so a hung await (your stalled model stream) suspended the very machinery that should have timed it out. Second, a backstop alarm firing while that loop was wedged hit a re-entrancy guard that consumed the wake without re-arming it — that's the single `alarm ~35s, outcome=ok, Logs=[]` line in your Logpush followed by total silence. The DO stayed alive holding the pending stream, so eviction-driven recovery never triggered either. Neither alive nor dead, exactly as you put it.

**What changed (on main, shipping in the next release):**

1. The Cloudflare coordinator was restructured: supervision (deadline enforcement, wake management) now runs as bounded storage-only passes that arm their successor wake *before* doing any failable work, and attempt execution runs detached — a hung attempt can no longer block its own timeout, and no single pass failure can break the wake chain. At `durability.timeoutMs` the attempt's abort signal fires (a stalled stream unwinds through it); an await that ignores its signal is settled over after a 60s grace. Either way you get a durable `submission_settled` record and a live `failed` event with `error.type: 'submission_timeout'` — within roughly your `timeoutMs` + 30s.
2. Your exact trigger — a 200 that never speaks again — no longer waits for the deadline at all: model streams on the binding provider now carry an idle timeout (default 5 minutes, configurable via `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `cloudflareBindingProvider`) that fails the turn as a *retryable* interruption, so it retries under the transient-error budget. Given your control turns succeeded in 7–11s, the retry would almost certainly have answered around 00:36 instead of nothing at 00:44.
3. `requestTimeoutMs` on the gateway options is now actually wired (emitted as the `cf-aig-request-timeout` header). Note its real semantics per Cloudflare: it bounds time-to-*first*-response, complementing the idle deadline rather than replacing it.
4. Tools that ignore their abort signal are now abandoned rather than awaited (the orphaned work's eventual result is discarded), and `observe()` deliveries are handed to `waitUntil` so a settlement emitted at the tail of an invocation can't be dropped mid-POST to your bridge.

**Your questions:**

1. *Should durability timeout always emit a host-visible failed/aborted event with the submissionId?* Yes — it now always does (live event + durable record). Not doing so was the bug.

**Correction to my own report: the trigger I described is wrong.**

I claimed above that the trigger is instructions naming phase tools imperatively ("call `research_module`"), based on variants B/C (clean) vs D (reproduced). I tested that directly by rewriting D's instructions as goals instead of orders, changing nothing else. It made nesting **worse**:

| Instruction wording | Task the worker can complete? | nested calls | max depth reached | depth errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| imperative (`Call \`research_module\`…`) | **yes** | **0** | — | 0 |
| imperative | no | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| goals (no tool names) | no | 2 | 3 | 0 |
| goals (no tool names) | no | 3 | **4** | **5** |

So variant D was a **confounded** reproduction — it varied wording *and* task answerability together. The real variable is the top row: with a task the worker could actually complete, the *imperative* wording produced zero nesting and a completed pipeline.

**The trigger is the model being unable to make progress.** Stuck, it falls back to the one thing its inherited instructions describe — the whole pipeline — and re-enters. In my repro the worker couldn't research the subject (bare project, no files); in the real application the phase couldn't satisfy its result schema.

**This makes the report more serious, not less.** If wording were the trigger, applications could avoid it by writing prompts differently. They can't. Any multi-phase agent is exposed the moment the model gets stuck, and being stuck is normal.

**What still stands, unchanged and independently verified:**

- A `harness: true` tool's conversation receives the parent agent's entire tool registry (variant A: it calls the parent's harness tool, nesting to 4).
- It inherits the parent's system prompt verbatim (variant C: the tool asked its own harness conversation to echo it, and got the agent's text back).
- `tools: []` does not restrict it — identical recursion, since the option is additive.

**A measurement pitfall worth adding to the observability list.** Counting `Maximum delegation depth (4) exceeded` occurrences does not measure re-entry: nesting only errors if it happens to reach 4, and two runs above nested with **zero** errors. Combined with nesting being invisible in the event stream (every nested conversation reports `session=default`), there is no supported way to observe re-entry at all. I had to wrap each tool body in an `AsyncLocalStorage` frame and log whether a frame was already active, which is how the table above was produced.

**An application-side workaround that does work,** for anyone else hitting this: wrap each `harness: true` tool's body in an `AsyncLocalStorage` frame and throw if a frame is already active when the tool starts. Measured results — nesting capped at depth 2, zero depth errors, and the model recovers by taking a different route rather than looping.

Two details for anyone copying it: `AsyncLocalStorage` **does** propagate across the `harness.prompt()` boundary, so a nested tool sees its parent's frame. And a plain boolean flag is not sufficient — models legitimately issue several phase tools in one turn from root, and those are siblings, not nesting; a flag refuses them, ALS does not.

Given wording is not the lever, the useful upstream fixes narrow to: rejecting a harness tool re-entering itself at dispatch (never intentional, no schema or tools-block change, so no prompt-cache impact per the reasoning in #522), and putting depth plus the invocation id on events so this is observable without patching application code.

The tools most likely to hang on us were the ones the sandbox integration injects (`bash` in particular); `LocalSandboxOptions` is currently `cwd`/`env` only. A host-level default that also applies to sandbox/channel-contributed tools (or a way to configure/override those tools' definitions) would close the gap the host can't reach today.

**Design note 2 — for subprocess tools, settling the call isn't enough.** Racing `run()` against a deadline bounds the *submission's* loss, but the orphaned child keeps running — holding ports, files, and pipes — unless something reaps it. An `AbortSignal` into `run()` only helps if the tool's internals observe it *and kill the process group*. Following up on my earlier comment with two more findings from running flue 2.0.3 in production with a `local()` sandbox — both in the bash/exec timeout path, both verified against the shipped code.

**1. A bash timeout discards all collected output**

When `createBashTool`'s timeout fires, it returns a synthetic result:

```js
const timedOut = () => formatBashResult({
    stdout: "",
    stderr: `[flue] Command timed out after ${params.timeout} seconds.`,
    exitCode: 124
}, params.command);
```

But the layer below has already done the right thing: the node adapter's `execShell` accumulates stdout/stderr as they stream, group-kills at the deadline, and **resolves with everything collected up to the kill**. The tool layer then throws that result away — `if (timeoutSignal?.aborted) return timedOut()` discards the resolved `result` object that contains the real output.

Where this bites: a test suite prints its results at second 10, then a leaked handle (an unclosed server, a dangling socket) keeps the process alive past the deadline. The agent receives `Command timed out after N seconds.` and *nothing else* — the pass/fail evidence existed in a buffer and was deleted, so the model's only move is to rerun work that already succeeded. For agent workloads this matters a lot: the timeout is most likely to fire on exactly the commands whose partial output is most valuable (long test runs, builds).

The fix looks one-line-shaped: format the real result and append the timeout notice, rather than replacing it —

```js
if (timeoutSignal?.aborted && !signal?.aborted) {
    return formatBashResult({
        ...result,
        exitCode: 124,
        stderr: `${result.stderr}\n[flue] Command timed out after ${params.timeout} seconds.`,
    }, params.command);

```

(with the catch-path fallback keeping the current synthetic result for adapters that reject on timeout).

**2. The node adapter dropped pi's post-exit grace timer, so orphaned pipes burn the full deadline**

Flue's `execShell` settles on `close` — pipe EOF. When a command backgrounds a child and exits (`node serve.js &`), the parent shell exits in milliseconds but the grandchild inherits the pipes, so `close` never fires: with no timeout the call hangs forever (this was our original incident upthread), and *with* a timeout it burns the entire deadline even though the direct child exited almost instantly.

Upstream-of-upstream already solved this: `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core`'s `waitForChildProcess` (harness/env/nodejs.ts) handles exactly this shape with `EXIT_STDIO_GRACE_MS = 100` — on child exit with streams still open, it arms a 100ms idle timer (re-armed by any late data), then destroys the streams and settles with the exit code. Same command returns in ~100ms under pi's env versus a full deadline under flue's `execShell`, which reimplemented the wait without that behavior. Porting the grace timer would make the deadline a true worst-case bound instead of the common-case cost for this shape.

For what it's worth, we've shipped both behaviors downstream without forking, via the `SandboxFactory.tools` seam: a wrapper that never passes `timeout` to `createBashTool` (so the discard path never arms) and enforces the deadline in a proxied `sandbox.exec` instead — kill semantics and output formatting stay flue's, and the partial output survives. That's evidence the output-preserving change composes cleanly with the existing adapter contract. Happy to turn either or both into PRs if there's interest.

Reporting this as a problem rather than a patch, per CONTRIBUTING.

I instrumented `SqlStorage` to count the actual base64 characters pulled from
`flue_submission_chunks` during a reconcile pass, rather than inferring residency
from row counts. With 5 pending submissions of 512 KiB each, one session apiece:

    listRunnableSubmissions()  ->  2,621,440 base64 chars hydrated

That is the full 5 x 512 KiB, materialised on every pass.

The part that makes it look purely wasteful rather than a tradeoff: I traced every
consumer of `listRunnableSubmissions()` on both platforms and none of them read the
payload.

- `cloudflare/agent-coordinator.ts:740` — uses `submissionId` only
- `node/agent-coordinator.ts:419` — uses `submissionId` only
- `node/agent-coordinator.ts:1267` — uses `.length` only

All three then re-read the row through `claimSubmission`. So the hydrated payload is
loaded and discarded on every wake, and the byte cost buys nothing for these callers.

Two related observations while I was in there:

1. `listRunningSubmissions` and `listUnreadySubmissions` hydrate the same way, so a
   single reconcile pass pays this cost three times, not once. Fixing only the
   runnable list reduces the crash loop rather than removing it.
2. A lazy `input` getter looks like an easy fix and is not one. Non-caching
   re-hydrates unboundedly across the loop; caching grows monotonically through it.
   Either shape is subtle enough that I would not want it landing without tests, and
   the repo currently has none — which is also why I measured bytes directly instead
   of trusting a row count.

Happy to leave it here. If a byte-free ref shape is the direction you want, note that
five external adapter packages implement this store (libsql, mongodb, mysql, postgres,
redis), so an additive optional method lets adapters without it keep today's
byte-carrying payloads.
